svg.title: Renal pathways: clear parallel rows, no crossing connectors

g.text: Read one row LEFT → RIGHT. Repeated structures are the SAME structures. No lines connect different rows or panels.
Solid arrows = forward pathway. Red dashed local return = negative feedback. A–H group related pathways; row IDs replace long cross-links.
Important structures / receptors / proteins / sites retained. Intracellular second messengers and phosphorylation sites omitted.
A1 Osmotic input via SFO / OVLT
VP production and release are different sites. Renal actions continue in B1–B2.
A2 Intrinsic osmosensitivity of VP neurons
PVN / SON can sense osmotic change as well as receive SFO / OVLT input.
NEGATIVE FEEDBACK: Osmolality restored → osmotic thirst stimulus ↓.
A4 Low osmolality: reverse water response
NEGATIVE FEEDBACK: Removal of excess water resolves the low-osmolality stimulus.
NEGATIVE FEEDBACK: Corrected osmolality reduces osmotic VP drive.
Requires a functioning medullary gradient (G). AQP2 is a water channel, not a pump.
UT-A1 transports urea; water extraction still requires AQP2. See G3–G4.
NEGATIVE FEEDBACK: Restored filling / BP reduces the depletion-related VP stimulus.
* Retained as the lecture model; net renin also depends on perfusion, NaCl delivery and feedback.
C1 Low volume → atrial receptor unloading → VP
NEGATIVE FEEDBACK: Filling restored → atrial stretch / firing recovers → non-osmotic VP drive ↓.
Brainstem routing follows the lecture’s simplified integrated baroreceptor model.
C2 Low arterial BP → arterial receptor unloading → VP
NEGATIVE FEEDBACK: BP restored → arterial firing ↑ → NTS / CVLM ↑ → RVLM / VP drive restrained.
C3 RVLM → sympathetic cardiovascular and renal outputs
NEGATIVE FEEDBACK: BP recovery reloads arterial receptors → RVLM / sympathetic drive ↓.
Separate renal sympathetic branch: JG β₁† → renin (D3).
C4 Higher filling / BP → reverse reflex
NEGATIVE FEEDBACK: As excess filling / pressure resolves, the initiating stretch stimulus declines.
Normal BP does not imply zero VP: osmotic inputs remain active.
NEGATIVE FEEDBACK: Restored renal perfusion reduces the JG renin stimulus.
Restored NaCl delivery reduces this input. Macula densa signals; JG granular cells release renin.
This is a renal branch of the sympathetic output in C3 / E5.
NEGATIVE FEEDBACK: ANGII inhibits further renin release: short-loop feedback†.
Aldosterone is made in adrenal cortex and acts on the distal nephron.
Restored volume / perfusion reduces renin–ANGII drive (D1).
This converges on the same VP system as A and C; repeated nodes are the same structures.
Pressure / perfusion recovery reduces renin drive (D1); this action does not require a brain relay.
Parvocellular PVN → RVLM is distinct from magnocellular PVN / SON → posterior pituitary.
Aldosterone does not insert AQP2. Water retention depends on available water / permeability.
NEGATIVE FEEDBACK: Restored K⁺ reduces direct K⁺-driven aldosterone stimulation†.
ANGII also stimulates this aldosterone-sensitive K⁺-secretory apparatus (E1).
This is the lecture’s compartment-buffering schematic, not an additional endocrine relay.
VP mainly regulates water permeability; aldosterone mainly regulates distal Na⁺ / K⁺ transport.
Plasma [Na⁺] is a concentration. Total-body Na⁺ strongly influences ECF volume.
AQP2 is apical; AQP3 / AQP4 provide basolateral water exit.
UT-A1 / UT-A3 transport urea. NKCC2, ENaC and ROMK transport ions.
Magnitude / timing also depend on renal perfusion, delivery, gradient and water availability.
G1 Countercurrent multiplication: build the NaCl gradient
Longer loops support a greater gradient. NKCC2 is bumetanide-sensitive; it is a cotransporter.
G2 Countercurrent exchange: preserve the gradient
Vasa recta preserve the gradient; they do not create it.
G3 Water reabsorption promotes passive urea exit
Urea moves down its concentration gradient; VP increases UT-A1-mediated permeability (B2).
G4 Use the gradient to make concentrated urine
Both permeability AND the osmotic gradient are required. High VP alone cannot replace a lost gradient.
Intact thirst and access to water can keep plasma Na⁺ near normal despite polyuria.
This is a renal-response defect, distinct from low VP production / release.
Hyponatraemia is water excess relative to solute; it does not require primary total-body Na⁺ depletion.
BP rises chiefly through volume expansion; serum Na⁺ need not be high. K⁺ loss can cause weakness / arrhythmias.
Low renin is not present in all chronic renal disease. Hyperkalaemia can cause cardiac / muscle effects.
VP = ADH / vasopressin. PVN = paraventricular nucleus; SON = supraoptic nucleus; MnPO = median preoptic nucleus.
SFO = subfornical organ; OVLT = organum vasculosum of the lamina terminalis. These sensory CVOs detect osmotic / circulating ANGII information.
NTS = nucleus of the solitary tract; CVLM inhibits RVLM. CVLM / RVLM = caudal / rostral ventrolateral medulla. JG = juxtaglomerular.
MR = mineralocorticoid receptor; AT₁ = ANGII type-1 receptor. CD = collecting duct; TAL = thick ascending limb; ECF = extracellular fluid.
* VP–macula-densa V₁a–NO / PGE₂ is the source lecture model, not a universal prediction that VP increases net circulating renin.
† Supporting connections: JG β₁, direct K⁺–aldosterone feedback, ANGII inhibition of renin, and distal acid / NH₄⁺ handling.
Source: Dr J Chu, BBMS2006 (Renal — student version), PDF pp. 3–15, 19–46, plus the relevant classroom supplements. One complete overview; details selectively retained.
